newsitem.title: USA: Consumer prices muted in June, output rises steadily.
newsitem.headline: Consumer prices muted in June, output rises steadily.

text.p: Consumer prices barely rose in June while factories churned out a rising volume of goods with no sign of strain, economic reports showed Wednesday, helping restrain inflation to its lowest level in a decade.

The reports sparked a major Wall Street rally that fired stock prices to a record close and sent interest rates plummeting as investors bet the Federal Reserve would see little pressure to raise interest rates soon.

The Labour Department said the consumer price index rose a scant 0.1 percent in June, the fourth consecutive 0.1 percent increase. So far this year, cheaper energy and low food price increases have limited the CPI's rise to an annual rate of just 1.4 percent, the smallest gain for the first half of a year since 1986.
Last year the CPI rose 3.3 percent.

The so-called core rate of price rises, which cuts out volatile food and energy costs, also rose just 0.1 percent in June. In the first half of 1997, the core rate gained at a 2.4 percent annual rate, the slowest in 32 years.

The chairwoman of the White House's Council of Economic Advisers, Janet Yellen, hailed the prices report as further proof that an economic expansion was rolling solidly along in its seventh year with no sign of dangerous price rises to derail it.

"This report, together with last Friday's report on producer prices, indicates that inflation remains well under control," Yellen said. Producer prices dropped for a sixth straight month in June, the first time that happened in the 50-year history of the wholesale prices measure.

Separately, the Federal Reserve said industrial production increased 0.3 percent in June after a revised 0.2 percent rise in May. The U.S. central bank said new cars rolled off assembly lines at a brisker clip in June while production of commercial aircraft, computers and other high-technology products maintained a robust pace.
Businesses ran at 83.5 percent of capacity last month, indicating little difficulty for them to boost output using their existing plants, factories and work forces.

"I think what this is telling us is that there's almost a complete lack of inflationary pressures in the economy," Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc., said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Investors celebrated the wealth of favourable economic news.

The Dow Jones industrial average surged 63.17 points to close at 8,038.88 -- the first time it has ever closed above 8,000 -- and the 30-year Treasury bond jumped almost a full point, lowering its yield to 6.48 percent from 6.55 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
A week before Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan is scheduled to deliver his semi-annual assessment of the economy to Congress, prospects appeared glowing for sustained growth.
Some members of Congress, while praising the Fed for its deft management of interest-rate policy, used the occasion Wednesday to lobby for a continued hands-off policy.
"Inflation is nowhere to be found," said Jim Saxton, chairman of the Joint Economic Committee, noting commodity prices were sluggish, the dollar was strong and long-term interest rates were steady.
"All of this suggests the Federal Reserve has little remaining reason to be considering rate hikes," Saxton said, a view that was widely shared by Wall Street analysts.

Economist Josh Feinman of Bankers Trust Co. in New York said the industrial output report confirmed that manufacturers could boost output without much strain and hence there was no need for higher rates.
"There is nothing in here to get in the way of the market feeling that the Federal Reserve is on hold and the good times can continue," Feinman said.

The Fed held short-term rates steady at its last two meetings in May and earlier this month after raising them in March, the first increase in more than two years. Fed policy-makers are next set to meet on Aug. 19.
A separate Commerce Department report showed a modest rise in business inventories in May as sales fell at the sharpest rate in nearly a year.

Stocks of unsold goods rose 0.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $1.02 trillion after a revised 0.4 percent gain in April, the department said. Sales fell 0.5 percent in May after a 0.2 percent pickup in April.

Department officials said it was the largest drop in monthly sales since a 0.7 percent fall in June 1996, a sign that consumers spent less in the second quarter, further reducing potential price pressures.
